en: Homage to the Buddha, who is the secret treasury of non-dual vajra and the destroyer of evil views.
I shall explain the destruction of false views according to the rules for the initial practice;
by this very mode of conduct and through diligent effort, one attains the state here in this world. May beings—both those in training and those beyond training—uphold this.

In this regard, it is established that for those in the causal state who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), there occurs the attainment of the excellence of perfect enlightenment through the accumulation of the two provisions, by means of performing extremely pure and other such deeds;

and for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whose conceptualizations regarding the reality of the fruit and its opposing factors have been eliminated, the uninterrupted initial activity characterized by working for the benefit of sentient beings proceeds indeed through the power of the momentum of their former vows and through the yoga of simultaneous effortless application, just as in the case of the Sage of the Śākyas.
And thus, O Lord, you have no conceit, no conceptual construction, and no discrimination;
yet, through effortless spontaneity, your Buddha-activity proceeds in the world.
This is considered the most preeminent fruit of those who have attained the perfection of the welfare of others.
Whatever else there is, such as Buddhahood and so forth, is considered the fruit because it serves that purpose;

like a wish-fulfilling gem, it is unshakable by the winds of all conceptual constructions. Nevertheless, it fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings without exception, for its fruit consists in the removal of the obstacles to reality through the abandonment of both affirmation and negation.
The fortunate one awakens to perfect enlightenment; thereafter, however, how is it that the prescription of initial rites for those in training (śaikṣas) is indeed appropriate?
How so?

Even for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who have realized the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the undertaking of a first action is in truth nothing other than being bound by golden shackles.
Because it is devoid of the realization of the perfection of wisdom,
for the perfection of wisdom is indeed the intrinsic nature of the five perfections; for this very reason, it is called "emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects."
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"The five perfections, when devoid of the perfection of wisdom, do not receive the designation 'perfection,'" as also stated in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
Skillful means devoid of wisdom is bondage; wisdom devoid of skillful means is bondage. Skillful means accompanied by wisdom is liberation; wisdom accompanied by skillful means is liberation.
Furthermore, their identity is understood as being spontaneously established through the teaching of their union, just like a lamp and its light.
For this very reason, it is said: "A beginner, as well as all yogis, should perform what has been prescribed."
That gnosis which is sought for enlightenment is inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
Furthermore, the five perfections are declared to be "initial action" by the designation of "initial action," yet among these,
the perfection of wisdom is not held to be their essential nature.

And so it is said: "The wise man who constantly and respectfully practices generosity, ethical conduct, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom becomes happy and healthy even while alive;
for generosity, ethical conduct, and patience are the causes for the creation of enjoyment."
"Meditation and wisdom" is considered by both [the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas] to be the vigor of the Dharma,

which destroys wrong views; therefore, a bodhisattva should become one who dwells in perfectly pure preliminary practice, for otherwise there would be the consequence of falling into nihilistic views regarding error.
As it has been said: "Although the auspicious and the inauspicious are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvaka*), one should nevertheless perform only what is auspicious, not what is inauspicious.
In the conventional world, which is like the reflection of the moon in water, pleasure is dear and suffering is perpetually unpleasant.

How then can there be the initial engagement of those among the trainees (*śaikṣa*) who abide in the vow of the madman (*unmattavrata*) and possess resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in non-conceptuality?
It is said:
having performed the gift of the body,
and having given the gift of the body, one should afterwards undertake the vow (cāṃ).

According to this statement: generosity is that which is given until the end of the body; ethical discipline (*śīla*) arises from the restraint of body, speech, and mind for the sake of all sentient beings; patience (*kṣānti*) consists in enduring being cut by saws and the like; vigor (*vīrya*) consists in enduring the non-affliction of the eight worldly dharmas; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) consists in proceeding spontaneously and effortlessly regarding all intrinsic natures; and wisdom (*prajñā*) consists in the realization of the characteristic of the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
When there is the penetration of the flavor of effortlessness, all the supreme perfections proceed without obstruction.
Therefore, even for those established in the conduct of the insane, the initial rite (*ādikarman*) indeed proceeds;
however, the speech of the Cārvāka beast—who has lost the next world—is not cited at all because it is entirely illogical.
The *poṣadha* is first granted by the Bodhisattva to one who is a *bhūtaśaikṣa*.

Following that, regarding the instruction on the precepts, according to the words of the venerable Hevajra: first, the bestowal of the *poṣadha* [vows] is as follows: "Pay attention, Venerable Preceptor! I, who am named so-and-so, an upāsaka, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha until reaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Thus, a second and a third time.
"Thus, may you bear in mind that they shall hold me as one who has gone for refuge, saying:

'I, the lay follower named so-and-so, from this time until the rising of the sun tomorrow, in the interval between now and then, abstain from killing any living being, from taking what is not given, from unchaste conduct, as well as from divisive speech, falsehood, intoxicants that cause heedlessness, eating at improper times, wearing garlands and using perfumes, dancing, singing, and music, and from high beds and seats; today I refrain from these, and I undertake them. These are the eight branches of the *poṣadha* verses."

The householder bodhisattva, however, who is preceded by taking refuge in the Triple Gem, abstains from the five [transgressions]: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, and the drinking of intoxicants—which are naturally reprehensible. Endowed with learning and discernment, this householder bodhisattva has abandoned the ten unwholesome actions and possesses the vow of non-repetition; practicing virtuous deeds, he should rise during the morning watch, perform his cleansing of the face and other such duties, and while recollecting the Three Jewels, protect himself through yoga with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, and then engage in meditation, recitation, praise, and so forth, according to his realization.
One should recite the *Nāmasaṅgīti* three times a day;
following that, having consecrated water with the mantra *oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*, one should offer one hundred and eight mouthfuls of the water to Jambhala.

Then, having recited seven times the mantra: *namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvatathāgatāvalokini oṃ sambhara sambhara haṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should visualize that from the five fingers of the extended right hand, five streams of nectar flow forth, filling the water-offering bowls (*sikyakas*) containing food offerings placed at the base of the door. These have been prepared by a Magadhan measure of one *droṇa*. Having offered this dense mass of clouds to all the *pretas* and *piśācas* within, one should present the *bodhisattva-bali*.

Now, having cultivated toward all sentient beings a loving-kindness (*maitrī*) characterized by the affection one feels for an only son; a compassion (*karuṇā*) whose nature is the desire to rescue them from the ocean of saṃsāra, from suffering and the causes of suffering; a sympathetic joy (*muditā*) whose power arises from a mind uplifted by taking refuge in the Three Jewels; and an equanimity (*upekṣā*) marked by the eradication of attachment and wrong views—one whose mind is intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings...

Having prepared a small maṇḍala—either square or any other desired shape—on a consecrated ground with cow dung, pure water, and the mantra *oṃ āḥ vajrarekhe haṃ*, one should visualize Akṣobhya in its center: black in color, holding the earth-touching gesture (*bhūsparśamudrā*), and arisen from a blue syllable *haṃ* atop a sun-maṇḍala within the pericarp of a multicolored eight-petaled lotus. Then, on the eastern petal, one should visualize Vairocana: white in color, holding the gesture of awakening (*bodhyaṅgīmudrā*), and arisen from a white syllable *oṃ*. Next, on the southern petal, Ratnasambhava: yellow in color, holding the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*), and born from a yellow syllable *cāṃ*. Then, on the western petal, Amitābha: red in color, holding the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhimudrā*), and produced from a red syllable *hīḥ*. Finally, on the northern petal, Amoghasiddhi: green in color, holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), and arisen from a green syllable *baṃ*. Having thus visualized them, one should consecrate everything with the mantra *oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ* and present whatever is most desirable.
These five Tathāgatas are clothed in saffron robes, wear turbans, and have their heads and faces shaved; they are situated within circles of light.

Vairocana is within a supreme lunar disc, while the other four face Akṣobhya, and Akṣobhya faces the practitioner. In front of them, reciting this verse of the Three Refuges as it has been received, one should say: *Namo buddhāya gurave | Namo dharmāya tāyine* || 1 ||
Homage to the Great Saṅgha; homage always to the Three Jewels as well.
The Triple Gem is my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly. I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I produce the sublime mind of awakening and invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of awakening so that I may become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.

Confession of all misdeeds, rejoicing in all merits, and the observance of the fast—I shall practice the noble eightfold poṣadha. Then: with bodies anointed with the sandalwood of ethical discipline, and clothed in the mantle of meditative concentration.
Having recited, "Scattered with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, may you dwell as you please," one should dismiss [the deities] with "Oṃ vajramaṇḍala muḥ.
In this same manner, one should worship Mañjuśrī and the others according to the instructions.
The Ritual Procedure for the Mandala Offering.

By performing the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections: giving is cow-dung mixed with water; morality is sweeping; patience is the removal of dogs and ants; vigor is the application of effort; meditation is making the mind focused on that very moment; and wisdom is the bright, well-drawn lines. One becomes golden-colored, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, and possesses a radiant splendor like the moon.
Having performed the bodily actions in this supreme abode of the Sugata, one is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
This is the verse on the benefits of the mandala.
Having prepared a mandala every day with flowers, cow dung, and water,
one should offer something to the guru at the three times of the day with devotion;
furthermore, one should avoid causing displeasure in the minds of others and maintain satisfaction within one's own mind.
Happy, gracious, and fortunate, he is born in Sukhāvatī;
there shall be the destruction of wrong views,
the fulfillment of the six perfections, and he will be sustained by the Buddhas and others.
He who, endowed with infinite virtues, constructs the maṇḍala—
such are the benefits.
Having correctly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* according to the ritual procedures for the mandala and so forth, one should worship it constantly; for that purpose,
one should immerse oneself in its meaning, whether it be a single verse, four verses, or the *Gāthādvitaya-dhāraṇī*.
With a concentrated mind, having undertaken the Six-Syllable mantra and the Bhadracaryā prayer, from the time of three periods until the next three periods,
the wise one— maintaining his vows without break— should recite them according to what he obtains, up to the limit of one hundred thousand.
One should also worship paintings, books, images, and so forth of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of paintings and books.

Now, according to the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra*, the procedure for the all-encompassing striking is extended by analogy: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ vajrapuṣpe svāhā*—this is the mantra for taking the earth.
*Oṃ vajrodbhavāya svāhā*.
The mantra for bowing to Vimbabala is: Oṃ araje viraje svāhā. The mantra for anointing with oil is: [Oṃ araje viraje svāhā].
Oṃ dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā, the mantra for casting the mudrā;
Oṃ vajram unnarākoṭana svāhā.
The mantra for striking is: Oṃ dharmarate svāhā. The mantra for summoning is: [Oṃ dharmarate svāhā].
Oṃ apratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā. This is the mantra for installation. Oṃ sarvatathāgatamaṇiśatadīpte jvala jvala dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā.
The consecration mantra: Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhe āhara āhara āgaccha āgaccha dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā. The dismissal mantra: [Oṃ] visarjaya visarjaya gaccha gaccha svabhāvaviśuddhe svāhā.
Oṃ ākāśadhātugarbha svāhā. This is the mantra for requesting forgiveness. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for all forms of striking.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vairocanaprabharāja, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. It is thus: Oṃ, subtle one, most subtle one, equal one, equanimous one, peaceful one, tamed one, established in composure, without support, traverser, possessed of fame, of great splendor, in the untroubled nirvāṇa, empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, svāhā! Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over a lump of clay or a lump of sand, one should fashion a caitya.

"As many atoms as there are in that [image], so many millions of caityas have been made; one obtains merits numbering as many atoms, becomes a lord of the ten stages (daśabhūmīśvara), and will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vairocana.
This concludes the section on the shared great benefits.
"Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

Having established oneself with this verse, one should perform the veneration of the *caitya* with the following: "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaketurāja! That is to say: Oṃ ratne ratne mahāratne ratnavijaye svāhā!"
By this dhāraṇī, through the single act of bowing to one caitya, it becomes equivalent to bowing to ten million caityas.
This is the procedure for constructing caityas from clay, sand, and other materials.

One should dedicate this by means of the great dedication taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, thinking: "When dedicated by this most distinguished method of dedication, it becomes the bringer of fruit, which is the eradication of all distinguished wrong views."

That is to say: just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas know and see with their Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye that root of merit—its extent, its category, its kind, its characteristics, its intrinsic nature, and the reality (*dharmatā*) by which it is known—I rejoice in that root of merit accordingly; and just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas authorize that root of merit being dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so do I dedicate it.
Furthermore: "By this wholesome deed of mine, may I become a Buddha before long in this world;
may I teach the Dharma for the benefit of the world, and may I liberate sentient beings who are oppressed by manifold sufferings."
The Procedure for Rejoicing in and Dedicating Merit.
Whatever one's livelihood may be, one who lives purely should earn it;
one should regard it as medicine intended for the sake of patience and the alleviation of illness.
Then, to those who have gathered there, one should offer the *bali* with the mantra: *Oṃ akāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt oṃ āḥ hrīḥ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) with the mantra: *Oṃ āḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyo vajranaivedye hrīḥ*.
Having recited: *Oṃ hārīti mahāyakṣiṇi hara hara sarvapāpān śrīṃ svāhā*, one should give two morsels of food to Hārītī.
Reciting "Svāhā to those who eat the first morsel," one offers the first morsel.
Thereafter, having empowered one's own food with "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," one should first touch it with the ring finger and thumb for the sake of pacifying defects such as poison, and then eat.
After eating as much as is comfortable, one should offer the leftover food with: "Oṃ, Svāhā to those who eat the discarded morsel."
One should offer the discarded morsel (utsṛṣṭapiṇḍa) and abandon the remaining food without any further intention;
likewise: "One should offer the oblation (bali), the food offering (naivedya), and the first morsel to Hārītī."
One should give the fifth [offering], which has been set aside for the enjoyment of great fruit.

Thereafter, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and other rites, one whose intellect is completely purified should recite this three times for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings who are endowed with distinguished bliss: "May the king, the patron of the gift, and all other multitudes of sentient beings always attain happiness, longevity, health, and prosperity."
Thus, thereafter, having purified his actions of body, speech, and mind, he should dwell as he pleases;

subsequently, having sat down, he should spend each day or day after day together with spiritual friends— whether they have come to him or not— by means of discourses on generosity as taught in the *Jātaka-nidāna*.
Then, even at the evening twilight, one should perform meditation, recitation, praise, and so forth, with a mind undaunted according to one's understanding.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with *yugakāra*, one should sleep in the yoga-sleep (*yoganidrā*).
How is the term "lay practitioner" (*upāsaka*) to be understood?
Diligent in the worship of the Buddha, resting in perfect tranquility,
he should be endowed with skillful means for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus, one should always avoid evil and association with the most wicked; restraining a person from sin, one should cause them to confess their transgression in every respect.
Thus, liberated from all superimpositions and perfectly concentrated in meditative absorption, the wise one, ever possessing supreme bliss, shall accomplish awakening.
One who says "ka" always exerts effort and maintains compassion; even through hardship, they do not do what is undesirable, but rather performs the highest service.

According to this statement, this lay follower (upāsaka), who possesses these four syllables, has eradicated wrong views, abandoned unwholesome actions, and accumulated a store of merit; by the power of his practice, he performs only wholesome deeds even in dreams, just as he does in the waking state.
Seeing the world as resembling a reflection— pure and undisturbed—
one should act toward everything like a magical illusion, through non-apprehension.
Therefore, he is called "irreversible.
Thus, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, he should remain until reaching the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), accumulating an accumulation of merit continuously day and night;
by name he is Gaganagarbha, devoted to the meaning of the Middle Way.
The beginner, being concentrated, indeed makes the formal undertaking.
This beginner’s manual was composed by me at the request of a noble Brahmin of virtuous intent who arrived from Vajrapīṭha.

Indeed, here, at the request of Gaganagarbha, I have spoken this "Destruction of Afflictions" (Kleśanirghāta) by means of a few words concerning the preliminary practices (ādikarma). By practicing it, one will soon remove the darkness of sin and attain the awakening of a stainless intellect.
Whatever merit I have gained by performing these preliminary practices—may that [lead to the welfare of all beings].
Having performed this initial rite, may the world attain excellence.
The *Kudṛṣṭinirghātana* is hereby completed.

In this regard, there are three stages: the causal stage (*hetvavasthā*), which extends from the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) until reaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);

the resultant stage (*phalāvasthā*), which consists of the state of having produced the knowledge of perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi-jñāna*) and the attainment of the abandonment of all afflictions and the acquisition of all virtues;
and the stage of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyāvasthā*), which extends from the first turning of the wheel of Dharma until the disappearance of the teaching.

In the *Ayavaccasaṃgraha*, that [compassion] has three states of the cause: the state of intention (*āśayāvasthā*), the state of application (*prayogāvasthā*), and the state of mastery (*vaśitāvasthā*).
Among these, the state of intention is the vow not to abandon sentient beings.
Its causes are four, namely: the causes of [proper] sphere, good friends, compassion, and fearlessness regarding suffering.
By these four conditions, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is produced.
According to this statement,
the state of attainment consists of ten stages,
and its application is twofold.

For one whose mind is characterized by resolute conviction, there are seven perfections; therein, for one who practices through resolute conviction, there are ten perfections: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and primordial awareness—these are considered the ten perfections.

For one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*), the gift is endowed with four perfections—namely, the perfection of intention, application, recipient, and the object given. Likewise, ethical discipline, tranquility, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, along with skillful means (*upāya*)—these seven perfections (*pāramitā*) are superior to those practiced during the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā*). Thus, there are two types of the state of application (*prayogāvasthā*).

Furthermore, there are five masteries (*vaśitā*), namely: mastery over afflictions (*kleśa*), rebirth (*upapatti*), karma (*karman*), skillful means (*upāya*), and the maturity of sentient beings (*sattvaparipāka*).
In that regard, one who abides in the causal state must perform all preliminary practices (*ādikarmma*);
however, for one who abides in the resultant state and the state of performing the welfare of sentient beings—such as Śākyamuni himself—the preliminary practice proceeds spontaneously (*anābhogena*).
This should be understood in detail from the *Kudṛṣṭinirghāta*.
Having bowed to Mañjuśrī— the root downfalls, the gross downfalls, and the non-abiding nirvāṇa, beautiful with joy for the world— I shall speak of the fourteen root downfalls.
By showing contempt for teachers, by transgressing the commands of the Sugatas, by speaking out of hatred against the qualities of the Buddha-field, and by abandoning great loving-kindness;

In the abandonment of the thought of awakening, in the disparagement of the vehicles and the mandalas, in the disclosure of secrets, in taking sides with [the wicked], and in the reviling of the Conqueror, the self, and the aggregates;

In doubt regarding the pure nature of the self and phenomena, in the desire for what is desired and in the absence of detachment, in the superimposition of non-self upon phenomena, and in the defilement of the faithful mind—these are [the causes of decline].

If one fails to practice the commitments, fails to attain them, or defiles a woman who is the embodiment of wisdom, a root downfall occurs; therefore, the practitioner of mantra must observe the commitments.
If one acts for his sake, there will be no accomplishments; rather, it is a heap of suffering. He experiences the state of hell and various intense torments.

Then, having performed worship of the guru according to what has been received, one should take up the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and the vows of the Three Jewels and so forth within the mandala.
The root downfalls are completed.
Through attachment to the service of the Vidyā, through failure to observe the commitments (samayas), through quarreling at the gaṇacakra, and through the disclosure of secret teachings;
He taught the sublime Dharma to those beings of faith, lest they fall into error; he dwelt for seven days in the midst of the great assembly of Śrāvakas.

Through union with one who is not a consort, or by using an unsuitable vessel, or by revealing secret places, a gross transgression occurs; therefore, the yogin must maintain the vow of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Having honored the great teacher with offerings according to one's ability, one should confess the transgressions of the vows with an unhidden mind.
The grave offenses are concluded.
In the *Aḍayavaccasaṃgraha*, titled *Tattvaratnāvalī*: Homage to the venerable Vañcasattva!
Having bowed before the two lotus-feet of Vajrasattva, whose radiance is as stainless as the autumn moon, we shall now proclaim the *Tattvaratnāvalī*.
For those whose vision is obscured by the darkness of having fallen away from the true tradition, this *Tattvaratnāvalī* correctly illuminates the reality for men.

Furthermore, there are four vehicles—the Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekayāna, Mahāyāna, and [the fourth]—and thus there are four established systems. These are distinguished as Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka.
Among these, the Śrāvakayāna and Pratyekayāna are explained according to the Vaibhāṣika system.

The Mahāyāna is twofold: the Pāramitānaya and the Mantranaya. Among these, that which is the Pāramitānaya is explained according to the systems of the Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka; however, the Mantranaya is explained according to the systems of the Yogācāra and Madhyamaka.
The Yogācāra is of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of *sākāra* (with aspects) and *nirākāra* (without aspects).

Likewise, the Mādhyamika is also of two kinds, distinguished by the proponents of the "illusion-like" (*māyopama*) and the proponents of the "non-abiding of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-apratiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, the Śrāvaka is of three kinds, distinguished by the categories of inferior, middling, and superior.

In this context, the "weak" and "middling" [positions] belong to the Western Vaibhāṣikas, while the "intense" belongs to the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas. Regarding that, the commentary explains that the weak Śrāvaka’s investigation consists in first apprehending external objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, and then asserting the person's (pudgala) dissociation from permanence and impermanence.
As it has been said: "Indeed, there exists [the notion] 'blue' and so forth—[a notion] which is supreme in its depth and its dread of the seizure by the demon of grasping at entities."

"There exists a person who carries the burden"—I do not say this is permanent, nor do I say it is impermanent. Furthermore, because the person, possessed of passion, wanders in saṃsāra, the meditation on impurity is considered for the sake of its complete abandonment. One should contemplate the body as a collection consisting of feces, urine, semen, blood, phlegm, mucus, tears, saliva, spittle, spleen, liver, and so forth.
As it has been said: "First, separate this leather bag from your own intellect; with the sword of wisdom, strip the flesh away from the jar of bones."

"Even having separated the bones one by one, look at the marrow within; consider for yourself: what essence is there here? Thus, the prior superimposition regarding the eternity of the person (*pudgala*) is a defilement of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[The view is: "As long as I live, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha"—thinking, "O Friend, O Sugata, O Elder," until such time as I shall subdue that single self through my roots of merit, I shall discipline that single self, I shall become composed in that single self, and I shall bring that single self to final nirvāṇa. This is the [false] view.

The view of the middling [practitioner] is as before; however, he has some inclination toward the welfare of others. His meditation consists of perceiving the person (pudgala) as devoid of permanence and impermanence through the concentration on inhalation and exhalation (ānāpāna-samādhi).
Through the retention of breath (kumbhaka), there is a state of motionlessness, which is an impurity of concentration because it induces dullness.
For the superior śrāvaka who does not accept external objects, there is the establishment of the selflessness of the body;
the commentary [on this] consists of the thorough knowledge of the four noble truths, the vision of the emptiness of the person, and meditative concentration.
Herein, suffering is to be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the origin [of suffering] and must be abandoned; insight (*vipaśyanā*) is the cessation and must be realized directly. The path consists of the superimposition of the nature of *sadāśiva* upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is the essence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); furthermore, its specific distinction lies in performing the welfare of others (*parārthakāritā*).
Regarding this, some maintain that the Śākyabuddha alone is the inferior *śrāvaka*, because his sphere of activity is fixed and he lacks compassion.

"All shall become Buddhas; there exists no one on earth who is incapable [of it]. Therefore, one must not despair in the pursuit of perfect enlightenment. Thus, they believe that even a Śrāvaka of mild disposition among sentient beings will become a perfectly enlightened Buddha, though he does so by depending upon a certain Buddha as his fixed field of reference.

The middling [practitioner] is one who will become a pratyekabuddha in the future; the superior [practitioner], however, is capable of the wisdom and insight (*jñāna-vipaśyanā*) of four incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

In that regard, the cessation of the faculties (*indriya-nirodha*) is insight (*vipaśyanā*), which is the non-apprehension of a person (*pudgala-anupalabdhi*) and the capacity for the restraint of body and speech. This is his meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
In this context, meditating on the state of happiness of the mind when sleep is imminent, and meditating on the state of deep sleep of the mind, are both impurities of *samādhi*.
Regarding these, the former involves entering the view of Bhāskara;
as it has been said: "When sleep has not yet arrived and the external object-field has vanished, one should diligently cultivate that state of the mind which then occurs."

But in the other case, there is an entry into the Vaiśeṣika doctrine; as the venerable Nāgārjuna said: "Knowledge that is unaware is established by the analogy of sleep; that knowledge which arises when the senses have ceased is considered the Vaiśeṣika view. The teaching of the Blessed One is also: "I would rather become a jackal in the delightful Jeta Grove than attain the liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas, O Gautama! The [Vaiśeṣika] view is also as before.

This one also brings about the state of Buddhahood, which is not to be established for four *kalpas*. Furthermore, the compassion of these two—the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha—is based upon sentient beings. That compassion which arises day after day by taking hold of sentient beings through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) is the compassion based on sentient beings; this is the verbal teaching of the Śrāvaka, whereas for the Pratyekabuddha it is physical.
As it has been said: "In the absence of the appearance of Perfect Buddhas and the disappearance of the Śrāvakas, the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddha arises from solitude."
Now, the practitioners of the Pāramitā system are described. Among them,
the Mṛdu-sautrāntika maintains that an object consisting of an accumulation of atoms indeed produces a cognition endowed with an aspect (sākārajñāna).
And its very nature of reflexive awareness (*pratyavekṣatā*) is this, namely, that it is the producer of a cognition with an image (*sākārajñāna*).

Regarding this, they say: "If it is asked how [an object] at a different time can be grasped, those who know the reasoning understand that its state of being an object consists precisely in its capacity to impart its form to the cognition. Thus is the commentary.
For one whose collection of senses has turned away from sense-objects, meditation is the state of being beyond thought;
as it has been said: "The time spent in the practice of Sāṃkhya is the reckoning of action; therefore, one should cultivate familiarity with it."

And as for familiarity: when one practices with awareness after having fixed the mind, then one does not perceive the mind; where has it gone, or where could it abide? One who has attained the leisure of a householder should meditate, assuming the vajra posture and fixing the flickering mind on the tip of the nose. The impurity of this samādhi is as before.

Through the non-apprehension of mental constructs (*citayānupalabdhyā*), one practices the five perfections with the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-svabhāvena*). Since there is no turning away from the fruit, there is no dedication for the sake of sentient beings, because of the view of that [fruit]. This is the middle Yogācāra.

In that regard, among those who maintain that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākārajñānavāda*), even an atom is untenable according to the reasoning [stated in] the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "By means of the six [atoms], the atom is joined simultaneously," and so forth.

One has realized that "this world is indeed of the nature of consciousness alone; it appears as luminosity, bearing the forms of consciousness and being entirely free from the state of grasped object and grasping subject.
Thus it was said: "O Son of the Victor, the triple world is nothing but consciousness!
And likewise, the venerable Kīrti[pāda] said: "If the intellect itself possesses the form of blue and so forth, what would be the basis for an external object?"
"If cognition (*dhi*) does not possess forms such as blue and so forth, what would be the basis for an external object?
Thus it has been stated elsewhere: "By their very nature, the objects of the senses do not exist externally within cognitions;

rather, it is consciousness itself that appears through the manifestation of form and so on. Therefore, consciousness alone—possessing its own cognitive form and being manifest independently of anything else—is what shines forth. This is the exposition of the Yogācāra who maintains the theory of cognition with aspects (*sākāravijñānavādin*).
However, the Yogācāra who maintains the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravādin*) considers that this very mind is of the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) without forms.
As it has been said: "An external object does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish;
rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object. And whatever appears, that appears only as an illusion."

"In reality, it is indeed without appearance, resembling the pure and infinite sky; the Dharma-body of the Great Sage is free from conceptual elaboration and without appearance, while the two form-bodies (rūpakāya) arise from it and subsequently remain like an illusion. This is the explanation: for the proponents of the Sākāra-vāda, meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization of the non-duality of true consciousness, in which all conceptual constructions have been dispelled.
As it has been said: "To whatever object the mind goes, one should apply [the awareness] to that very object;
having moved, where could it go? For everything is indeed composed of that.

Thus, for the proponents of formlessness (nirākāravādins), meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization of the mind as being without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), beyond thought, and free from the conceptualization of the two [subject and object].
And so it is said: "The nature of this [reality] is considered to be pure, without parts, and stainless;
it can never be known by one who lacks awakening. For, according to the *Tattvaratnāvalī*, this [world] is indeed nothing but consciousness alone, as is established through direct perception.

He would not establish anything [else], for he abides by that alone. But when no object of cognition is perceived at all, then one stands firm in the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratva*), because there is no grasping when there is no graspable object. In this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the eternally real, ultimate cognition with its form, there is an entry into the position of the Vedāntins; for they maintain that the world is ultimately real, eternal, and a transformation non-different from Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness.
And so it has been said: "Whatever is seen, one should conceive that as Brahman;

thereby the mind does not go elsewhere, but abides in Brahman alone. Thus, the impurity of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) belongs specifically to the proponents of the theory of forms (*sākāravāda*).

Similarly, for the proponents of the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*), there arises the undesirable consequence of entering into the position of the Vedāntins who follow the school of Bhāskara, insofar as they cultivate a self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana-vijñāna*) that is eternal, devoid of appearances, and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

He too accepts that within me—the ocean of consciousness—there exists the pure, dense mass of light and bliss, eternally Brahman, free from the defilement of the entire proliferation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*). That reflection [of the world] therein, whether arisen or dissolved, does not lend itself to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus ends the section on the impurity of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of those who maintain the doctrine of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*).
The views are as before: the superior and the middling.

Regarding that, the exposition of those who propound the non-dual simile of illusion is as follows: "It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither."

The Madhyamikas know reality to be free from the four extremes. And this is its meaning: it is not existent, because that would entail contradiction; nor is it non-existent, because of its manifestation. Likewise, due to the fault of duality, it is neither both. Because of the higher realization—that form within consciousness is according to the power of things as they are, yet there is no attachment—this is indeed the "illusion-like" state; such is the explanation.
And the cultivation of this very [reality] which is like an illusion is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Any adherence to annihilation therein is merely a stain on that concentration;
for through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that all phenomena are like an illusion, there is the vision of the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

For those who maintain that all phenomena are without foundation, this is their investigation: The universe is not held to be eternal, nor is it intended to be annihilated; neither the pair of eternity and annihilation, nor that which is other than both, nor that which is not both. The wise know the reality of things to be established upon everything; yet this conceptualization does not exist at all, for consciousness knows neither the state of being consciousness nor the state of being non-consciousness. As long as there is any superimposition, none of it exists in any way whatsoever.

In the meaning of the Middle Way there is no superimposition; how, then, could there be a method for ascending to it? For that knowledge which is effortless is declared to be inconceivable; indeed, that which is conceived as inconceivable cannot truly be inconceivable. By means of pure wisdom, the wise one understands the world to be unborn; thus, through effortlessness, the world is his own reality. As it has been said: "When the true nature itself shines forth, entirely free from all superimpositions..."

By means of designations such as "emptiness," there is the removal of superimpositions regarding that [reality]. And for this object—which has come under investigation and is of a non-superimposed nature—one should realize it through dwelling in non-adherence; this is meditation (*dhyāna*). The cutting off of all objects is insentience (*jaḍībhāva*), which is the stain of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Through non-superimposition, there is the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); this is the view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Here, in the weak and middling stages, compassion (*karuṇā*) has phenomena (*dharma*) as its objective support.
Compassion that has phenomena as its object arises by taking as its support all phenomena that fall into the calamity of impermanence;

this is to be understood as the compassion of one who possesses superior resolve, which has as its object the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and does not take as its object the realization of phenomena characterized by mental constructs (*manas-tattva-ratnāvalī*).
And the establishment of his body's accumulation has been stated by the Lord Maitreya as follows:
"That by which he performs various benefits for the world equally, until the end of existence, is the uninterrupted emanation-body (nairmāṇika-kāya) of the Sage."
This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, is considered the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya), which partakes in the Mahāyāna.
The nature of those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects is the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) of the Sage.
Thus it is said.

As for the Mantra system (*mantranaya*), however, it is not explained here by those such as ourselves because of its extreme profundity, because it is intended for persons who have faith in the profound method, and because of the extensive detail in the revelation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) such as the four seals (*caturmudrā*).

And so it is stated: "Even though the goal is one and the same, the Mantra scripture is distinguished [from others] because it is free from confusion, possesses many means, is not difficult to practice, and is intended for those with sharp faculties."
Furthermore, we have composed a treatise titled *The Ascertainment of the Madhyamaka* (*Madhyamakālaṃkāra*).
Now, one might ask: "If the ultimate reality is indeed that which is determined by the Mahāyāna, for what purpose did the Blessed One then teach the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles?

This is not so; it is precisely for the sake of leading others to the attainment of what is to be reached through the Mahāyāna that he fashioned the two ladders of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
As it has been said: "This method of the Perfectly Awakened One was fashioned like a staircase for the purpose of leading beginner beings to enter into the ultimate truth."

It is also said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: "There is indeed but one vehicle, and one is the method; this teaching of the Leaders is but one. Such is my skill in means that I display various vehicles as vehicles."

The venerable Nāgārjuna also said: "O Lord, because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is undifferentiated, there is no distinction among meditative absorptions; yet the three vehicles were taught by you for the sake of introducing sentient beings [to the path]."
Furthermore, it has been said: "Liberation is the vision of emptiness; for that purpose, there is the cultivation of all [dharmas].
And this illumination of the three vehicles should be understood by you, O Blessed One, as being non-empty.
For instance: "Not even a single syllable was uttered by you, O All-pervading Lord, yet the entire world of Māyā-people was satiated by the rain of the Dharma."
Unshakable like a wish-fulfilling gem by the winds of all conceptual thoughts, yet it fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings without exception.
Through the application of the wheel’s rotation, even though the Protector is free from conceptual construction, the teaching proceeds by the power of his accumulated merit and wisdom.

There is indeed no finality of vehicles as long as the mind continues to function; but when the mind has undergone revolution, there is neither vehicle nor traveler. This stainless garland of jewels of the True Dharma is here strung together in words; O wise ones, let it be placed in your hearts for the sake of joy.
However, because I desire brevity, I have condensed this most excellent [work] out of affection; those who love detail should forgive me for this.

Having composed this unsurpassed treatise through diligent application of the method for the sake of those capable of liberation, may the world, by whatever merit has been gained thereby, attain the unattainable state of a Tathāgata.
The *Tattvaratnāvalī* is completed.
This is the work of the scholar-paṇḍita Avadhūta Ādya-Vajrapāda.
[Also included here is] the *Pañcatathāgatamudrāvivaraṇa*.
Homage to the All-Knowing One!

Born dependently, empty of conceptual construction, and empty of intrinsic nature, they do not exist as substantial entities; yet, being neither annihilated and having the singular nature of consciousness, the five Victors—form and the rest—are triumphant.
The five aggregates are the five Tathāgatas.
Why, then, are four [of them] sealed by Akṣobhya for the purpose of demonstrating that they are mere gnosis?

By this it is shown that when external objects do not exist, due to the emptiness of the grasper, consciousness alone—which is devoid of both grasped and grasper and is the ultimate reality consisting of pure awareness—remains.
This very stainless state, resembling the midday sky, is the fundamental knowledge to be established for the proponents of formlessness (*nirākāravādin*).
As it has been said: "Empty of imagined forms, free from appearances, and without shape; it is indeed pure existence, consciousness, and bliss alone, untroubled by a collection of external forms."
As it has been said: "The latter two, however, are the form-bodies (rūpakāya).

And likewise: "The Dharma-body of the Great Sage is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and devoid of appearance (nirābhāsa); the two form-bodies arise from it and subsequently remain as mere illusion."
[Objection: Since [Akṣobhya] is already established by the mudrā alone, for what purpose, then, is Akṣobhya sealed as the nature of the vajra? [Response:
If you say it is for the sake of demonstrating the emptiness of all imagined forms, that is not so, because he is already established by the previous mudrā alone.

Therefore, just as with the Akṣobhya-mudrā, the primary gnosis is the principal [form] while the other is secondary, so too with the Vajrasattva-mudrā, consciousness (*vijñāna*) would be secondary and the *vajra* the principal.
And it is said in the *Vajraśekhara*: "Firm, essential, heroic, characterized by being uncuttable and impenetrable, neither burning nor perishable—emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called the *vajra*."
Thus:
if form and so forth are in the back, then because that is not known, would that *sattva*—which is [produced] by the consort Akṣobhyamudrā—not also be in the back?
If you say that it is the *sattva* that is in the back, then, due to the absence of compassion, there would be the consequence of falling into nihilism (*ucchedavāda*).

And it is asserted: "By *vajra* emptiness is expressed; by *sattva*, the nature of mere gnosis. The identity of these two is established through the essence of Vajrasattva. The distinction between emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light; the unity of emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light. Emptiness is not other than phenomena, nor do phenomena exist without it. This inseparable relation is like that between the produced and the impermanent. When reality is explained in this way, there is no annihilation of the conventional; yet reality is not perceived apart from the conventional."
Such is the detailed explanation.

If it is argued that Akṣobhya and Vajrasattva are thus identical, then the doctrine of non-dual diversity (*citrādvaitavāda*), which does not abandon the forms of consciousness and so forth, is superior.

As it has been said: "The accumulated [world] is pure consciousness alone, empty of all conceptual constructions; this is my view of the doctrine of having form (*sākāramata*). Others consider it to be like the touch of grass being stepped upon; the wise proclaim that to be the meaning of the Middle Way."
For those who propound the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaitavādin*), however, the notion that [this state] is ultimately real is unsatisfactory.
This is because the existence of a thing as a reality is negated by the *vajrasattvamudrā*—the cognition whose nature is the unshakeable non-dual variegation devoid of subject and object.

As it has been said: "If cognition is empty of conceptualizations such as form through the seal of Akṣobhya, then by the seal of Vajrasattva, its existence as a real entity is negated. Nor is the emptiness of the imagined aspect of mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*) produced by Vajrasattva, because that [mere representation] does not exist prior [to the realization]."
The Explanation of the Seals of the Five Tathāgatas:

Thus, when the thorn of [the notion that things exist] in an ultimate sense has been removed, this Madhyamaka tenet—which is established through the direct experience of non-abiding in all respects, effortless spontaneity, and the union of the two truths—is most excellent;
and this is understood through the grace of the feet of a true guru.

If it is argued that, upon the establishment of sensation, there follows the doctrine of non-duality resembling an illusion, and thus there is non-abiding everywhere—[we reply: that which is dependently originated has not arisen by way of its own intrinsic nature;
how then can that which has not arisen [inherently] be called "arisen"?
Thus, sensation is dependently originated; therefore, sensation itself is non-abiding and has not arisen as a state.
And so it is said: "Sensation is indeed unborn, and the existence of things is likewise."
The Sage proclaimed that the world itself is the very nature of Vajrasattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when asked by the Tathāgata, "What is this inconceivable realm?

Mañjuśrī replied, "That realm which is determined, which cannot be reached by the mind, which cannot be measured by the mind, and which is not to be realized through mental volition—that is called the inconceivable realm.
Moreover, Blessed One, the mind itself is the inconceivable realm."
For what reason?
Because in a mind that is no-mind, no mind is found;
for it is a mind devoid of mind through the realization of the mind as it truly is.
Moreover, every mode of activity is the inconceivable realm of the Blessed One.
It is also said elsewhere: "O you whose intentions are non-conceptual, whose mind is non-abiding, who are without recollection or mental attention, and who are without support—homage be to you!"
In the *Catuḥpradīpa*: That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn; for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty (*śūnya*); he who understands emptiness is heedful (*apramatta*).
In the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: "Indeed, when all delusion has been shaken off, whatever sign arises—that itself would be his delusion, like the impurity of cataracts."

And thus: "Lest there be a lapse from conventional reality, for this very reason the Sage, out of fear, does not shatter the Dharma of his teaching, for it is indeed liberated by having emptiness as its essence."
And it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The intrinsic nature is indeed unarisen from the beginning; it is truth, not falsehood. Furthermore:

"If the statement of emptiness were not the primary cause for distinguishing between the internal [Buddhist] and the external [non-Buddhist], then everything would be the same when analyzed, and the final conclusion (*kṛtānta*) would be made by those whose intellects long for the mere expression of emptiness."

And it is said: "Those who perceive suchness in accordance with the meaning of the Middle Way, having removed the emptiness of annihilation—they alone are the fortunate knowers of reality, provided that they have direct personal experience through consciousness."
As it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "Wherein the mind is cultivated as inseparable from emptiness and compassion—that indeed is the teaching of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

Therefore, because the five aspects (*pañcākāra*) are dependently originated and possess the nature of the five Tathāgatas, and because that nature is inseparable from emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā*), it is established that the world is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion.
This very [realization] is meditation uninterrupted by means of the instruction of a true guru— like the continuous flow of a river's current or the succession of the light of a lamp—
in accordance with the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*).

And thus the venerable Nāgārjuna said: "This triple world is not a gabled palace, nor are these people living beings; the Lord of the Wheel here is not a human, nor are there sense objects, nor senses, nor forms and so forth. Since they are mandala deities by virtue of having the nature of reality (dharmatā), you who perceive the entire universe as the maṇḍala-circle—why, O mind, do you wander in delusion?"

Precisely because it lacks independent origination, the universe is clearly not established by way of its own intrinsic nature, like a body made of fragrance; nor is it non-existent, like a lotus in the sky.
And it is said in the *Hevajra*: "These phenomena are indeed nirvāṇa, yet through delusion they appear as saṃsāra.
We pay homage to that which is the cause of the momentary nature of sentient beings, from whose differentiation joys arise for the sake of attaining awakening."
From that, there would be a subtle ripening; but in the third stage, it is characterized by a different nature.
Then, the "crushing" (vimarda) should be understood as resulting from the rejection of Haṭha-yoga.

If there is both initial perception (*ālocana*) and deliberation (*vimarda*), how can it be maintained that this occurs in the third [moment], since that which is initial perception would not exist at all, as cognition is devoid of characteristics [in that case]?

Therefore, it is logical that one who possesses a distinct characteristic [is fit] to kill or obstruct; in the third case, there would be the establishment of self-awareness, and the meaning of the scripture is also consistent.

For those [practitioners] for whom the "wondrous" occurs during kissing and embracing, the one named "ripening" occurs upon stroking, and the "extraordinary" occurs at the jewel, they possess the consciousness of difficult emission.
If that cognition which occurs regarding the "Jewel-treasury" were itself the reality, then it would be the Veda; however, this is not accepted by the Buddhists.
And so it is said, O Goddess, in that very *Nirnādatantra*, as you have asked: "O Goddess, this City of Jewels (*ratnapura*) should go to blaze within the filaments;
Rudra is the pair, the supreme Śiva, and Śakti is she who is higher than the highest."
Free from the characterized and the characteristics, and devoid of verbal expression,
a wondrous bliss arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Entities do not exist in reality as they are conceived through the form of causal powers;
rather, power is the vision of emptiness, which destroys all superimpositions.
From the union of Śiva and Śakti arises true bliss, the supreme non-duality;
yet neither Śiva nor Śakti exists [as separate entities], for they abide within the jewel like its inner luster.

In the chapter on Yoga as well, it is said: "For the yogi who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose, there is nothing whatsoever left to be done; if there were something to be done, he would not be a knower of reality."

Even for the Vedāntins, knowledge is held by Bhāskara to be supersensuous and non-apprehension; however, for Bhagavad-dāsa and others, apprehension consists solely of bliss and serves as the means to the Lord.
That bliss of the Brahman-principle which arises from the agitation caused by the union with Śakti and culminates in the absorption of Śakti is called the bliss of Brahman (brāhma-sukha).
There is no arrival of sufferings there; it is uninterrupted bliss. Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is called liberation.
Whatever indeed is seen, one should conceive of that as an illusion;
then, with a mind free from other thoughts, one abides in Brahman alone.
What else can be attained through other forms of vision than the sight of the beloved, by means of which even a mind filled with passion attains nirvāṇa?
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood. Having abandoned that by which you abandon, abandon even that.
Also in the Bhagavad Gītā: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
The truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality."
Furthermore, if the mind is said to be unshakeable because it is empty of the grasped and so forth,
how is it [so] according to scripture, given the absence of the Vajrasattva-mudrā?
For what purpose is this taught by the teachers of the land as a rule?
This was previously revealed with the intention of providing consolation for the Tathāgatas.

Some describe that which is with form and without form as being within the *bola* (vagina) and in front of it, [respectively]; however, this is not the view of our Guru, who teaches the Middle Way (*madhyamā*).
Whether it falls today or tomorrow, or even into a skull-bowl, the reality within the intermediate state is not desired; rather, it is known from the mouth of the Guru.
How is it well-established that [the jewel] is known as "variegated" (*vicica*) and so forth?
The statement that it is "within the gem" and so on is perfectly consistent with the True Guru.
That which is intended for the preceptor and others through the purification of laughter and so forth is established by way of origination;
it is not [established] by virtue of an already-arisen nature.

From the "scarring" [stage] one should understand the reality of the Guru; from the "rubbing" [stage], the ripening of the jewel before one; and from the cessation of the "churning," one attains delight.
Having attained the action-seal (karmamudrā), one should meditate upon the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā);
above that is the great seal (mahāmudrā), from which the pledge-seal (samayamudrā) arises.
Blisses have their corresponding seals (mudrās), yet they exist without the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) through scripture,
self-awareness, and the instruction of a true guru.
From the *karmamudrā*, the ripening (*vipāka*) is the nature of the world;
its stability is the "beyond-characteristic" (*vilakṣaṇa*), and that is the "dissolution" (*vimarda*), the excellence of the world.
Non-abiding in anything at all is called Mahāmudrā;
because self-awareness is free from conceptual elaboration, there is no possibility of diversity and the like.
For that gnosis which is effortless is declared to be inconceivable;
indeed, that which is conceived as inconceivable would not truly be inconceivable.
But those who perceive suchness in accordance with the meaning of the Middle Way—
they are indeed the fortunate knowers of reality, provided that they have direct experiential awareness of it.
Whatever superimposition there is of everything, all of that does not exist in any way whatsoever;
the meaning of the Middle Way is free from superimposition—so how could there be any application of superimposition therein?

The conceit [of duality] occurs when there is no superimposition of knowledge and the object of knowledge, and not otherwise; everything is just as it was before, for it is not as the mind [perceives it].
By which the world is known as unborn and purified through awakening, his intellect is indeed pure;
for him, that world is self-arisen and real by virtue of effortless wisdom.
This conceptual construction, arising from cognition, has its relationship [to reality] unmanifested;
therefore, do not allow your mind to be deluded regarding this very state as being nirvāṇa.
He who stands upon the path of practice, who is neither incapable of the truth nor devoid of it,
and for whom there is no attachment to the fruits of worldly life— he attains the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
Just as the arrangement of blisses and so forth occurs in the action-seal (karmamudrā),
so too does it occur in the commitment-seal (samayamudrā) through the grace of the Vajra Master.
The action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is indeed the moving one; the dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*) is born of its maturation.
The great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is devoid of characteristics; the pledge (*samaya*) is the state of non-duality.
Those who do not know Mahāmudrā and practice only with the Karmamudrā fall away from the reality of the oral tradition; such yogins go to the Raurava hell.
The mudrās and the four moments are not understood at all until they touch the festival of the feet of the Lord of the Lord.
Having performed this correct consecration, free from the painful sprinkling of forceful methods,
may the merit I have thereby accomplished bring happiness to the world.
The *Sekananirṇaya* (the determination of initiation) [or its exposition] is completed.
Thus, having first prostrated to Vajrasattva, who is identical with pure primordial wisdom,
this lineage of mudrās is set forth in brief for the sake of one's own enlightenment.
For here, those of deluded minds, wandering through the lineage of the *mudrās*, roam the ocean of existence in suffering.
To enable them to easily realize the meaning of the four *mudrās*, the *Mahāsukha-sādhana* is established in accordance with the *tantra*.
As for the "four *mudrās*": the *karmamudrā*, the *dharmamudrā*, the *mahāmudrā*, and the *samayamudrā*.
In this regard, the nature of the *karmamudrā* is described.

"Karma" refers to the mental activity of body, speech, and mind; the *mudrā* that has this as its primary characteristic is the *karmamudrā*, whose nature consists of conceptual construction. Within that *karmamudrā*, joys (*ānanda*) arise, differentiated by the distinctions of the moments (*kṣaṇa*), because from the knowledge of the moments comes the knowledge of bliss, which is established in the syllable *Evaṃ*.
There are four joys: joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), innate joy (*sahajānanda*), and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*).

The statement, "Having observed the target between the supreme [joy] and the cessation [of joy], make it firm," is not consistent. There are four moments: the variegated (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the distinct (*vilakṣaṇa*), and the reflective (*vimarśa*).
In the case of the consecration (seka), it should be understood that the "distinctive" (vilakṣaṇa) state occurs in the middle;

furthermore, in Haṭhayoga, it should be understood that the stability of the "innate" (sahaja) and the "distinctive" states occurs at the end. This was taught by the Blessed One regarding both the consecration and Haṭhayoga.
All that is innate is designated as "innate" because it conforms to the shadow of the innate;
that is, the shadow of the innate brings forth knowledge similar to the innate.
The innate is the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
Therefore, there is no arising of the co-emergent (*sahaja*) within the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).
This is to say that the very nature of that which is called "co-emergent" is the characteristic of being unstained by any phenomena whatsoever.
Consequently, having obtained the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the fruit of quiescence (*niṣpanda*) arises.
Vibration similar [to the original] is non-vibration.
Similarity is as follows: for example, the reflection of a face cast in a mirror is not the face itself;
it is neither previously established nor newly produced. This is the four seals (*caturmudrā*).
That very reflection in the mirror is established as producing mere similarity; nevertheless, people, thinking "I have seen my own face," become satisfied through delusion.
In the same way, teachers who give bad counsel, having attained the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), produce satisfaction by thinking "the innate (*sahaja*) has been experienced.
And being thus satisfied, they do not even know the news of the *dharmamudrā*.
Without knowing the *dharmamudrā*, how can the so-called *sahaja* arise through a mere *karmamudrā* that is artificial?

From a cause of the same genus, only an effect of the same genus arises, and not from one of a different genus; just as a rice sprout arises from a rice seed, but not a *kodrava* grain. Likewise, from the non-artificial *dharmamudrā*, the non-artificial *sahaja* arises.
Therefore, the *dharmamudrā* alone is the cause;
[it is the cause] of the *mahāmudrā* by means of metaphorically attributing difference where there is no difference.
Why?

In that case, it was said by the Blessed One: "That divine [mandala] in the shape of the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable BAṂ, is the abode of all happiness, the Buddha, the jewel casket."

Because it reflects the shadow of the Buddha, the *karaṇḍaka* is the location, the support; therefore, for the woman who is the limb of action (*karmāṅganā*), the lotus is a mine of jewels consisting of a mass of bliss.

When that clear abode becomes entered within the jewel of the conventional bodhicitta by the *avadhūtī* through the union of the essences of the *bola* and *kakkola*, then the gnosis named *ṇika*, known as the supreme innate (*parasahaja*), arises.
That is not the vibration of the innate (*sahajanispanda*).

In its true nature, the triad of wisdom (*prajñā*), gnosis (*jñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*)—endowed with the four moments—is declared to be the fruit of the *niṣpanda* [state] in the empowerment (*seka*), in Haṭhayoga, and in the case of the *karmamudrā*.
This is the first section: The Instruction on the Flowing-forth of the *Karmamudrā*.

Oṃ. The Dharma-mudrā has the nature of the Dharmadhātu; she is beyond conceptualization, free from discursive thought, devoid of desire, and lacking origination. She is of the essence of compassion, supremely blissful, uniquely beautiful, and the means [to liberation].

By virtue of her continuous permanence, she is of the nature of the Innate (*sahaja*); she is non-different from Wisdom because of the innate arising of Wisdom. That which is thus described is called the Dharma-mudrā. Her other characteristic—like the rays of the sun in the darkness of ignorance—is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru as being equal to a blade of grass, yet free from the sleep of delusion.

The entire world, which is of a single nature with the earth, water, wind, and fire, and which is undifferentiated from waveless emptiness and compassion, should be understood as being variegated by them all.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "Lalanā exists by the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and Rasanā is established as skillful means (*upāya*)."
In the central region of the *avadhūti*, free from the grasped and the grasper, even by one who is skillful,
the path should be known through the form of suchness as the proximate cause;
through the diligent and uninterrupted practice of the path within the knowledge of the path, there occurs the direct realization of cessation, which is the innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*).
And so it has been said: "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added;
one is liberated by seeing reality as it truly is.

Lalanā and Rasanā dwell in the region between those two; she who dwells there is Avadhūtī. For one whose mental state has attained the innate nature (*sahaja-svabhāva*) of all phenomena, the *Dharmamudrā*—by virtue of its essential form—is the cause for [attaining] the *Mahāmudrā* through non-differentiation.
The Second [Chapter]: The Exposition of the Ripening Fruit of the Dharma-Seal.
Āḥ! Regarding "Mahāmudrā": it is called Mahāmudrā because it is both great (*mahatī*) and a seal (*mudrā*).

This Mahāmudrā should be known as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvā*), free from the obscurations of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), resembling the sky at the clear midday of autumn, the support for all prosperity, having the single nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, embodied in non-referential compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), and having the single form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
And likewise: "Phenomena are unwholesome when not attended to; phenomena are wholesome when attended to.
In the Teaching, you are one whose conceptualization is non-conceptual, whose mind is non-abiding, who is without mindfulness or mental attention, and who is without support—homage be to you!
Regarding the four mudrās: that which is designated as the *mahāmudrā*—
by means of that *mahāmudrā*, whose nature is inconceivable, the fruit of the *samayamudrā* arises.
The Third [Chapter]: The Teaching on the Stainlessness of Mahāmudrā.

"Hūṃ—The Samayamudrā" means that which is taught as the Samayamudrā is the radiation of Vajradhara in the form of Heruka for the sake of sentient beings, by way of the nature of the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya, and in a translucent form.

And having taken up that *samayamudrā*, by conceptualizing the fivefold gnosis (*pañcavidhajñāna*) in the form of a wheel (*cakrākāreṇa*), the masters meditate upon the *samayamudrā-cakra* through the mirror-like, equality, discerning, activity-accomplishing, and perfectly pure dharma-realm [gnoses], and through the *ādiyoga*, *maṇḍalarājāśri*, *karmarājāśri*, *binduyoga*, and *sphuradyoga*.

By this, they become those who have performed merit, and consequently they do not fail to obtain the *dharmamudrā*, because of the statement: "From a determined cause, only a determined effect arises."
Therefore, through this nectar that is spontaneously accomplished, those things such as the fixed and the moving, or whatever else is imagined by the ignorant, attain the state of perfect awakening;
it is not through mantra-recitation, nor austerity, nor fire-offering, nor the mandala-deity, nor the mandala itself.
That is mantra-recitation, that is austerity, that is the fire-offering, that is the mandala-deity, and that is the mandala.
In brief, "the mind is of the nature of an assembly" means that,

in brief, all phenomena are of a single form— namely, the form of great bliss— and thus the mind, which is the *bodhicitta*, being of the nature of an assembly, or the gnosis in the form of the *dharmamudrā* and *mahāmudrā* empowerments, is designated as the "True Assembly."
The fourth chapter, the Exposition of the Fruit of Human Effort through the Samaya-mudrā, is completed.
In the *Adayavajrasaṃgraha*, the *Sekatānvayasaṃgraha* [states]:
Homage to the Buddha!
Even one who possesses the limbs of the auspicious path, if they do not grasp at meditative absorption (*samādhi*), is unrestrained.

Having understood from the Vajrācārya the compendium of the essential meaning of the consecration of true gnosis— which holds the unequal [teachings] of the sixth and fifth [families] like a reality held in the palm of one's hand— we shall compose various texts on the consecrations according to the scriptures.
The first is the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*); the second is the supreme secret;
the third is indeed the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*); and the fourth is likewise that again.
Its meaning is as follows: "the first is the vase consecration" refers to the six vase consecrations characterized by water, the crown, the vajra-bell, the name, and the master (*ācārya*).
One sprinkles external water upon the external body for the purpose of washing away the stains of ignorance; because one sprinkles (*siñcati*) with this, it is called *sekha* (sprinkling).

These are designated as the "Vase Consecration" (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) because they all involve the activity of the vase, and they are also the "Irreversible Consecrations" (*avaivartikābhiṣeka*) because they possess the nature of the six Tathāgatas.

For instance: the water-consecration consists of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and has the nature of Akṣobhya; the crown-consecration consists of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and has the nature of Ratnasambhava; the vajra-consecration consists of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and has the nature of Amitābha; the lord-consecration takes the form of all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) and has the nature of Amoghasiddhi; the name-consecration, through the cessation of ignorance, consists of the wisdom of the pure dharmadhātu accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*) and has the essential form of Vairocana; and the master-consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), however, has the nature of vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*).

And here, regarding the five empowerments (*pañcābhiṣeka*), because of the activity of the five vidyās beginning with Locanā upon the five [faces], the water empowerment (*salilābhiṣeka*) is to be bestowed by the Vajrācārya in the form of Akṣobhya upon the disciple who maintains the form of Vairocana, for the sake of washing away the stains of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, in all cases, there is the pride (*ahaṅkāra*): the future state of Buddhahood, which is the seed of the mindless *uṣṇīṣa*, is the collection of the lineage of the empowerment.
The crown consecration:
there, upon a vajra measuring twelve finger-breadths— which represents the purity of the twelve links of dependent origination—
is the syllable *haṃ*, which indicates the supreme state of reality (*niruttaradharmatā*) through its central rotation.

Its meaning is as follows: *ha* signifies being free from causes (*hetu-viyukta*), which is to say, devoid of conceptual construction (*ūhāpagata*); *aṃ* signifies that all phenomena are without foundation (*apratiṣṭhita-sarvadharma*).

Therein, sages in the form of flames radiate from the opening of the well of existence (*bhava-sara-ūṅga-mukha*). And *ghaṃ* signifies that through the purification of the aggregates (*skandha-viśuddhi*), they have emerged from the body of existence;
and here, by facing toward the center, above and below, all forms and so forth are indicated as being of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānātmaka*).

And in order to demonstrate that all these are of the nature of the All, they are everywhere square. Furthermore, those Buddhas of Dharma—who have realized the nature of the self as taught by the Lord and whose bodies are liberated from the five [skandhas]—are surrounded by other manifestations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is for the purpose of awakening [beings] everywhere. These are characterized by the perfectly pure dharmadhātu consisting of the five wisdoms (pañca-jñāna), which are the mirror-like, equality, discerning, and all-accomplishing [wisdoms], and they are to be known through the instruction of the Guru.

And the collective meaning [of the term] indicates indestructible gnosis: that which is firm, essential, non-perishable, characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible, unburnable, and imperishable—emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called "vajra.
Thus, in the *Hevajra*, it is said: "The indivisible is the vajra."

Observing the ritual procedure for this vajra-consecration (*vajrābhiṣeka*) as being like the implantation of the seed of indivisible gnosis (*abhedyajñānabīja*), the vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*) is likewise fashioned according to the previous intention: it measures twelve finger-breadths, and by means of its nature as the non-substantiality of the union of the downward-facing lotus and vajra, it is intended to demonstrate the nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmasvabhāva*). To awaken [the practitioner] to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) as the state of indivisible gnosis, it is adorned with two rows of vajra-garlands at the upper and lower parts. To proclaim that its nature is a celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) consisting of the three realms (*tridhātu*), it has the form of a *hāra* and *ardhahāra* necklace; for this very reason, it is marked with the five Tathāgatas. Furthermore, to communicate the cause of the gnosis that is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion, there is the manifestation of the face of transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, in order to explain that this gnosis, which is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, consists of the five Tathāgatas beginning with Vairocana, has the five aggregates (*skandha*) such as form as its intrinsic nature, and takes the form of the five elements (*dhātu*) such as earth, there is an arrangement of the five spokes above; here too, the intention regarding the central [deity] facing forward and so forth is as before.
Then, one should perform the consecration with this resounding vajra-bell.

Although the vajra-bell consecration is the instrumental cause—serving both to demonstrate preeminence here and to establish causality—it is surpassed by the first bestowal of the vajra consecration, which brings about the awakening to all dharmas without exception.

This is for the purpose of establishing that "all dharmas are nameless," and for the purpose of providing the introductory narrative for the future title appropriate to the state of a Lord of Sages; thus, by discarding the former name, the name-consecration is performed according to the specific deity family of the candidate.

And the Master’s Empowerment (ācāryyābhiṣeka) is characterized by the authorization of the Vajra-samaya, the Ghaṇṭā-samaya, the Mudrā-samaya, the fitness for instruction, the vows, the prophecy, and the consolation.
